Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder).

BUILD: a template / starter-prompt gallery.

## Why
The product opens on an empty prompt box. "Describe the site you want" is the blank-page problem — the single biggest drop-off in this category. A gallery of concrete starting points converts "I don't know what to type" into one click. It also steers people toward prompts the builder is actually good at, which raises first-build quality without touching the model.

## The hard constraint — read it before designing
Generated sites are single-page Vite+React+TS+Tailwind apps served under a strict CSP with **no backend of any kind**. Read `lib/agent.ts` (the SYSTEM prompt, in full) and `lib/foundation.ts` before writing a single template.

That means a template must NOT promise: working contact/booking forms, accounts or logins, carts or checkout, databases, external API calls, remote or stock images, custom web fonts, or multiple pages/routes. A "Booking site" template that implies real bookings is a lie that produces an angry customer. Templates for those verticals are fine ONLY if scoped to a one-page credibility site with `mailto:`/`tel:` link-out CTAs — and the template's own description must be honest about that.

Note also: `lib/agent.ts` was just given two new rules — never invent facts about a real business (use bracketed placeholders like `[your address]`), and never build a control that only pretends to work. Your template prompts should be written to cooperate with those rules, not fight them.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `lib/templates.ts`, `app/templates/`, AND `components/templates/`
Everything else is off limits — other agents are running in parallel. READ anything.

## What to build
1. **`lib/templates.ts`** — 18-24 templates. Each with: stable id, name, short honest description, category, and a **full, well-crafted starter prompt** (the thing that actually goes in the box). The prompt is the product here — write each one the way an expert user would: audience, purpose, tone, the sections wanted, and bracketed placeholders for facts only the owner knows. Cover the verticals the builder genuinely does well: restaurant/cafe, barber/salon, personal portfolio, photographer showcase (gallery of *placeholder* imagery — be honest that they can't upload photos yet), tradesman, gym/studio, law/accountancy, wedding/event info page, nonprofit, coming-soon/waitlist, SaaS landing page, product launch, personal blog-style single page, link-in-bio, agency, consultant, band/musician, local services.
2. **A gallery page** `app/templates/page.tsx` — browsable, filterable by category, each card showing name + description + a preview of the prompt. Clicking a template starts a project with that prompt prefilled.
3. **The hand-off mechanism** — read `lib/pending-prompt.ts` and how `components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx` and `app/(auth)/**` already move a pending prompt through signup into a new project (`PENDING_PROMPT_KEY`). Reuse that exact mechanism rather than inventing a second one. Signed-in and signed-out users must both work.

## Critical constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything else under lib/ (including agent.ts, credits.ts, events.ts, assets/**, pending-prompt.ts — read them, don't edit), app/api/**, app/projects/**, app/dashboard/**, app/settings/**, app/admin/**, app/legal/**, app/blog/**, app/page.tsx, app/globals.css, components/marketing/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- If the hand-off genuinely requires a change outside your scope, DO NOT make it — describe exactly what you need in your report instead.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies. DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Match the existing marketing visual idiom exactly — read `app/pricing/page.tsx` and `components/marketing/**` first. Restrained, monochrome with the brand gradient as accent, `rounded-2xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`.
- Accessibility: the public pages just went through an a11y pass. Match that bar — a `<main id="main-content">` landmark, a `SkipLink` (see `components/marketing/SkipLink.tsx`), real labels on the filter controls, visible `focus-visible:` states, no keyboard traps, and no horizontal scroll at 380px.
- **A known constraint you must respect: white text on the brand gradient fails contrast (worst 1.81:1). Do not add new white-on-gradient text.** Use the existing neutral button treatments instead.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components`; BOTH must be clean — the repo is currently at zero lint errors and must stay there.

## Report back
The templates you wrote, which verticals you scoped down for honesty and how, the hand-off mechanism you used, anything you needed outside your scope, and what you verified.

/**
 * Starter prompts for the gallery at /templates.
 *
 * The prompt is the product here, not the card. Each one is written the way an
 * expert user would write it — audience, purpose, tone, the sections wanted,
 * and bracketed placeholders for the facts only the owner knows.
 *
 * Every prompt is written to stay inside what a generated site actually IS
 * (see the SYSTEM prompt in lib/agent.ts and the starting files in
 * lib/foundation.ts): one Vite + React + TS + Tailwind page, served under a
 * CSP that blocks every external host, with no backend of any kind. So no
 * template may ask for — or imply — a working contact/booking form, an
 * account, a cart, a database, an API call, a remote or stock image, a custom
 * web font, or a second page.
 *
 * Where a vertical normally leans on one of those (bookings, RSVPs,
 * donations, checkout, waitlists), the prompt asks for a link-out instead — a
 * mailto:, a tel:, or a clearly-bracketed [link to your …] — and the card's
 * own description says so, so nobody clicks expecting a booking system.
 *
 * Two agent rules the prompts are written to cooperate with rather than
 * fight: never invent facts about a real business (hence the brackets), and
 * never build a control that only pretends to work (hence the link-outs).
 */

export const TEMPLATE_CATEGORIES = [
  "Food & drink",
  "Beauty & wellness",
  "Local services",
  "Professional services",
  "Personal & creative",
  "Startup & product",
  "Events & causes",
] as const;

export type TemplateCategory = (typeof TEMPLATE_CATEGORIES)[number];

export type Template = {
  /** Stable — it ends up in URLs and analytics, so never renumber these. */
  id: string;
  name: string;
  /**
   * One honest sentence. If the vertical usually implies a backend feature
   * this can't deliver, that limit belongs HERE, not in the small print.
   */
  description: string;
  category: TemplateCategory;
  /** The full starter prompt — exactly what lands in the composer. */
  prompt: string;
};

4. Hours and location, laid out so they are readable at a glance.
5. A footer with social links.

Leave every fact you cannot know as an obvious bracketed placeholder for me to fill in — [your address], [your phone number], [your opening hours], dish names and prices — instead of inventing something plausible.

There is no backend, so do not build a reservation form. The calls to action are a tel: link to [your phone number], a mailto: to [your email], and an optional [link to your booking system].

## Verticals scoped down for honesty
Restaurant/cafe/food-truck: no reservation or ordering form → `tel:`/`mailto:`/`[link to your booking system]`; food-truck schedule stated as hand-edited, no map embed. Barber/salon/gym: no booking engine or payments; button label must say "Call to book" rather than "Book now". Tradesperson/local services: explicitly no quote form ("a form that quietly loses an emergency call-out is worse than none"). Law/accountancy: no intake form, no client portal, no invented bar/SRA numbers, case results or testimonials. Photographer: card description says outright you cannot upload photos yet; the prompt asks for a designed placeholder-tile grid with captions instead of stock/remote images. Band: no embedded player — link out to streaming. Blog: no comments/newsletter/search; posts live in the page. Coming-soon: the prompt names the trap and forbids the email field, substituting `mailto:` with a prefilled subject or a link to Tally/Google Form. On click: write the (possibly edited) prompt to `PENDING_PROMPT_KEY`, clear `PENDING_PROMPT_IMAGE_KEY` (so a reference image attached on the home page earlier in the session can't ride along). Signed out → `router.push("/signup")`, where the existing "picking up where you left off" panel and `destinationAfterAuth()` in the signup/login submit handlers (and `/continue` for Google OAuth) take over. Signed in → call `destinationAfterAuth()` directly, then push its result. Either way `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` auto-fires the prompt on mount. The button stays locked after click so a double-click can't create two projects.

Giving them the template's name would need a change to `lib/pending-prompt.ts` (out of my scope), and would also only fix the signed-in path — the signed-out path goes through the auth pages' own call.
